title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every pair of nodes with LCA reconstruction versus a single post-order clamp-and-combine pass.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: A path in a binary tree is any non-empty sequence of nodes connected by parent-child edges, where each node appears at most once, and does not need to pass through the root. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum possible sum of any such path.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Any path, not necessarily through the root\"","Every node is a potential \"peak\" of some path; a post-order recursion tracking each node's best downward contribution, combined with a running global maximum, finds the answer"],["\"Values can be negative\"","A negative subtree contribution should be clamped to 0 (simply not used) rather than dragging the sum down"]]}

blocks.text: The best path passing THROUGH a specific node as its highest point equals that node's own value, plus the best (but never negative, since a negative addition would only hurt) contribution extending down into its left child, plus the best contribution extending down into its right child. But a node can only PASS UP one side's contribution to its own parent (a path cannot branch twice), so what a node returns upward to its own parent is its value plus the better single side (again, clamped at 0 if both are negative).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Most Profitable Trade Route Through Any Single Hub, Not Necessarily the Capital
blocks.text: Picture a trade network where profit flows from any hub down into either of two connected sub-networks. The most profitable route through a given hub as its central point equals that hub's own profit, plus the better contribution from each connected sub-network (skipping a sub-network entirely if it would only add losses), while what that hub reports UP to its own parent hub is its own profit plus only the SINGLE better connected sub-network, since a valid route cannot branch twice.

blocks.caption: The best path through a node uses its value plus its best (non-negative) contribution from each child

blocks.text: Maximum path sum = 42 (path 15-20-7, entirely skipping the negative root -10).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A path's highest point (the node closest to being a "root" for just that path) can be ANY node in the tree, not necessarily the actual root.

Observation 2: The best path through a specific node as its peak uses that node's value plus its best contribution from the left child AND its best contribution from the right child, each independently clamped to 0 if negative (since including a negative contribution would only reduce the sum).

Observation 3: However, what a node can legitimately report UPWARD to help its OWN parent form a longer path is its value plus only the BETTER SINGLE side (not both), since a path passing further up through the parent cannot also branch down both of this node's children (that would require the path to fork twice).

Observation 4: A single post-order recursive function can compute BOTH of these simultaneously: return the "upward contribution" value to the caller, while updating a shared global maximum using the "full path through this node" value as a side effect.
This leads to a single post-order recursive function returning each node's best single-side upward contribution, while updating a shared running maximum using both sides combined at every node.
Conceptually, try every possible pair of nodes as path endpoints, computing each candidate path's sum directly by finding the path between them.

# Conceptually: for every pair of nodes, find the actual tree path
# connecting them (via their lowest common ancestor) and sum its values
# directly, tracking the best sum found. Correct, but extremely wasteful:
# O(n^2) pairs, each needing path reconstruction and lowest common
# ancestor computation, when a single post-order pass finds the answer
# directly using the recursive structure of best-single-side contributions.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every pair of nodes directly implements the definition of "any path between any two nodes" literally.

This is extremely wasteful, needing lowest common ancestor computation and path reconstruction for every pair; a single post-order pass finds the answer using only each node's best single-side contribution, computed once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) or worse, considering all pairs and their path reconstructions.
Space: O(n) for path storage per pair.
Limitation: a single post-order recursion, tracking best single-side contributions and a running global maximum, finds the answer without ever considering pairs explicitly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Maintain a shared "best full path sum found so far" variable, initialized to negative infinity. Define gain(node) recursively: an empty node contributes 0. Otherwise, recursively compute the LEFT gain and RIGHT gain, each clamped to 0 if negative (max(gain, 0)). Update the shared best using node.val plus left gain plus right gain (the full path THROUGH this node, using both sides). Return node.val plus the LARGER of the two single-side gains (what this node can legitimately offer its own parent).
Use a single post-order recursion, returning each node's best single-side contribution while updating a shared running maximum with both sides combined.

codes.python:
def max_path_sum(root):
    best = float('-inf')
    def gain(node):
        nonlocal best
        if node is None:
            return 0
        left = max(gain(node.left), 0)                      # clamp negative contributions to 0
        right = max(gain(node.right), 0)
        best = max(best, node.val + left + right)              # full path THROUGH this node, both sides
        return node.val + max(left, right)                       # single best side, offered to the parent
    gain(root)
    return best

blocks.text: Clamping each side's contribution to at least 0 correctly reflects that a negative contribution should simply be excluded, never dragging the sum down; updating the shared maximum using BOTH sides combined correctly considers every node as a potential path peak, while returning only the SINGLE better side upward correctly respects that a path continuing further up through this node's parent cannot branch through both of this node's children simultaneously.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each node visited once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.

blocks.text: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum is a hallmark "combine both sides for the answer, but return only one side upward" recursive pattern, essential for correctly handling paths that do not pass through the root.

items: Returning the sum of BOTH sides upward to the parent (instead of just the better single side), which would incorrectly represent an impossible doubly-branching path to the caller.
Forgetting to clamp negative contributions to 0, incorrectly including a harmful negative subtree in the sum.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single node tree (possibly negative)","The answer is just that single node's value."],["All values are negative","The answer is the single LEAST negative node (the best \"path\" is just that one node alone)."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "combine both sides for the global answer, but return only the better single side to the parent" is the single most important detail that distinguishes a correct solution from a common bug here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "maximum path sum, path need not pass through the root", think: post-order recursion combining both sides for a running maximum, returning only the single best side upward.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The pairwise brute force costs O(n squared) or worse; the single post-order pass costs O(n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: post-order recursion combining both children's contributions for a running global maximum, while returning only the single better side upward.
Core Idea: clamp each side's contribution to at least 0; combine both sides for the full-path answer at every node; return only the better single side to the parent.
Time: O(n squared) or worse for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) per pair for the brute force, O(h) recursion depth for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a node can only pass ONE side upward, but both sides matter for the global answer at that node.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, hard recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: combine both sides for the answer, return only one side up.
